abstract: Milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) proteins are highly glycosylated and participate in various biological processes. However, the N-glycoproteomic profiles of MFGM protein in yak colostrum (YC) and mature milk (YM) remain unexplored. In this study, Astral data-independent acquisition proteomics was applied to analyze the MFGM proteomes of YC and YM, while 4D label-free quantification was used to investigate their N-glycoproteomes. A total of 4278 proteins were identified, of which 1271 were differentially expressed. Additionally, 89 N-glycoproteins, 120 N-glycopeptides, and 128 N-glycosylation sites were detected. Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes analyses showed many MFGM proteins and N-glycoproteins involved in immune functions, mainly enriched in pathways such as complement and coagulation cascades, Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis, and hematopoietic cell lineage. Findings from this research offer unprecedented perspectives on the MFGM proteomes and their glycosylation in yak milk and support the development of functional dairy products.

Materials and methods

Reagents

Formic acid (FA, ≥99.0 %, LC–MS grade) was obtained from Millipore (Burlington, MA, USA). Sequencing-grade trypsin was purchased from Promega (Madison, WI, USA). Acetonitrile (ACN, ≥99.9 %, LC–MS grade) was obtained from Merck (Darmstadt, Germany). H₂
18
O (95 atom%
18
O, isotopic grade), PNGase F (SDS-PAGE grade), Concanavalin A (ConA), wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), and lectin buffer salts (NaCl, CaCl₂, MnCl₂; analytical grade) were purchased from Aladdin (Shanghai, China). RCA120 lectin (biological reagent grade) was obtained from Vector Laboratories (Burlingame, CA, USA).
2.2
Milk sample collection and basic composition analysis
All experimental protocols were evaluated and endorsed by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Southwest Minzu University (protocol number SMU-202401158) and were conducted in compliance with EU Directive 2010/63/EU on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes. Fresh milk samples were obtained from healthy, grazing yaks in Hongyuan County (an altitude of approximately 3,500 m) in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau region. 15 multiparous Maiwa yaks with similar body weight, parity, body condition score, and overall health status were randomly selected for sample collection. All animals were managed under a traditional full-grazing system, with exclusive access to natural alpine meadows and ad libitum access to both pasture and water throughout the experimental period. Colostrum samples were collected within 2 h after parturition, while mature milk samples were collected on day 14 postpartum.
Milk samples from 15 healthy yaks were pooled into three pooled samples for colostrum and mature milk. For each pooled sample, milk from five randomly selected individuals was combined to minimize the influence of individual variation on the N-glycosylation of MFGM proteins (
Guan et al., 2023b
;
Zhong et al., 2024
). Each pooled sample was processed and analyzed independently to control for technical variance (
n
= 3). Upon collection, samples were promptly transported to the laboratory under dry ice conditions and subsequently subjected to −80 °C storage for further analysis.
The basic composition of pooled colostrum and mature milk was determined before MFGM isolation. Milk fat was measured by the Gerber method, protein content by the Kjeldahl method, and lactose content by the Lane–Eynon titration method, following standard procedures (
Sarkar et al., 2006
). Immunoglobulin G concentration was determined using a commercial ELISA kit (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
2.3
Extraction of MFGM proteins from YC and YM
The extraction of MFGM protein fractions followed a previously reported protocol with slight adjustments (
Lu et al., 2016
;
Yang et al., 2016a
). Samples were thawed at 4 °C for approximately 20 min until completely liquefied, and a 10 mL aliquot collected for processing was centrifuged at 3000 ×
g
(Centrifuge 5424R, Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany) for 15 min at 4 °C to isolate the fat layer, which was then carefully collected and mixed with 10 volumes of 0.1 M PBS. After thorough mixing, the sample was re-centrifuged at 3000 ×
g
for 10 min. The aqueous phase was discarded, while the fat layer was preserved. Subsequently, an equal volume of 0.2 % SDS solution was added, followed by thorough mixing and ultrasonic treatment for 1 min at 50 kHz using an ultrasonic system (150–96, Biosafer, Nanjing, China). The resulting sample was subjected to centrifugation at 12,000 ×
g
for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant obtained was retrieved as the MFGM protein fraction. Protein levels were quantified using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Waltham, MA, USA).
2.4
Digestion of MFGM proteins from YC and YM
A filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) approach, as previously reported by
Wiśniewski et al. (2009)
, was used for the digestion of MFGM proteins. Briefly, appropriate amounts of protein samples were reduced with DTT to a final concentration of 100 mM. The mixture was incubated for 5 min in a boiling water bath (JB Nova, Grant Instruments, Roysto, UK) and then naturally cooled to room temperature (approximately 25 °C) on the benchtop for about 10 min. Subsequently, 200 μL of uric acid (UA) buffer (pH 8.0, 150 mM Tris-HCl, 8 M urea) was added, and the mixtures were transferred to a 10 kDa centrifugal filter units (OD010C35, PALL, NY, USA). After centrifugation at 12,000 ×
g
for 15 min, the filtrate was removed. Additional UA buffer (200 μL) was introduced and subjected to the same processing conditions.
Following alkylation with 100 μL of 50 mM IAA in UA buffer, the samples were incubated for 30 min at ambient temperature before centrifugation at 12,000 ×
g
for 10 min. Two washes of the filters were performed with 100 μL of UA buffer, followed by another two washes with 100 μL of 50 mM NH₄HCO₃ buffer, each wash involving centrifugation at 14,000 ×gfor 10 min at 4 °C. Trypsin digestion was performed by adding 40 μL of trypsin buffer (6 μg trypsin in NH₄HCO₃) to each unit, gently mixing, and incubating at 37 °C for 16–18 h. The resulting peptides were gathered through centrifugation at 12,000 ×
g
for 10 min, acidified with 0.1 % trifluoroacetic acid, and desalted using a C18 solid-phase extraction cartridge (Sep-Pak® C18 Classic Cartridge WAT051910, Waters, MA, USA). Finally, peptides were lyophilized (AdVantage Pro, SP, Scientific, PA, USA) and reconstituted in 0.1 % FA for concentration measurement prior to liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis for subsequent Astral data-independent acquisition (DIA) analysis.
2.5
Glycopeptide enrichment and deglycosylation
After enzymatic digestion, appropriate amounts of peptides were transferred to new centrifugal filter units with a 30 kDa molecular weight cut-off (UFC503096, Millipore, MA, USA). Then, 50 μL of lectin mixture CWR (containing 90 μg each of Con A, WGA, and RCA120) was added to each sample (
Yang et al., 2016b
;
Zielinska et al., 2012
). After gentle shaking at 600 rpm (FastPrep®-24, MP Biomedicals, CA, USA) for 1 min, the samples underwent incubation at room temperature (approximately 25 °C) for 1 h, and then centrifuged at 14,000 ×
g
for 30 min. Four washes of the filters were then carried out using 200 μL of 1× binding buffer (pH 7.3, 2 mM MnCl₂, 2 mM CaCl₂, 40 mM Tris-HCl, 1 M NaCl), with centrifugation at 14,000 ×
g
for 30 min for each wash. Next, 50 μL of 25 mM NH₄HCO₃ in H₂
18
O were added, followed by centrifugation of the samples at 14,000 ×g for 30 min (repeated once). Afterward, 50 μL of 25 mM NH₄HCO₃ (H₂
18
O-based) containing 2 units of PNGase F were introduced into each filter unit for deglycosylation at 37 °C overnight. The next day, peptides were collected by moving the filters into new tubes and centrifugation at 14,000 ×
g
for 30 min. A further 40 μL of 25 mM NH₄HCO₃ (H₂
18
O prepared) was added and centrifuged again to recover residual peptides. Lastly, the collected peptides were lyophilized and reconstituted in 0.1 % FA for further analysis.
2.6
LC-MS/MS analysis of MFGM proteins and N-glycopeptides
All peptide samples were analyzed using a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system (Thermo Scientific, MA, USA) equipped with a trap column (PepMap Neo 5 μm C18, 300 μm × 5 mm) and an analytical column (μPAC Neo High Throughput). The mobile phases consisted of 0.1 % FA in water (solvent A) and 0.1 % FA in 80 % acetonitrile (solvent B), with a flow rate of 300 nL/min. For MFGM protein analysis, 1 μL of peptide sample (containing 500 ng peptides) was injected. The LC gradient was: 0–0.1 min, 4–6 % B; 0.1–1.1 min, 6–12 % B; 1.1–4.3 min, 12–22.5 % B; 4.3–6.1 min, 22.5–45 % B; 6.1–8 min, 99 % B. MS analysis was performed on an Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer in DIA mode with a total acquisition time of 8 min. For N-glycopeptide analysis, enriched peptides were analyzed under the same UHPLC conditions. The LC gradient was: 0–0.1 min, 4–6 % B; 0.1–1.1 min, 6–8 % B; 1.1–15.1 min, 8–22.5 % B; 15.1–20.6 min, 22.5–45 % B; 20.6–24 min, 99 % B. MS analysis was conducted in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode, with a total acquisition time of 24 min. Common MS parameters for both modes included: spray voltage of 2.2 kV in positive ion mode, full MS scan range of 380–980
m
/
z
, resolution of 240,000, automatic gain control (AGC) target of 500 %, and 3 ms maximum injection time. MS/MS settings were: 80,000 resolution, 500 % AGC target, 3 ms injection time, 40 % RF lens, 2 Th isolation window, and normalized collision energy (NCE) of 25 %. The cycle time was set to 0.6 s.
2.7
Database search
Analysis of the raw LC-MS/MS data was performed with two software platforms for proteome and N-glycoproteome identification. DIA MS data were analyzed via DIA-NN (version 1.8.1), whereas Proteome Discoverer (version 2.4, Thermo Scientific) with Sequest HT was utilized for N-glycoproteomic analysis (
Barkovits et al., 2020
;
Demichev et al., 2020
). Both analyses used the same UniProt
Bos mutus
grunniens database (uniprotkb-
Bos mutus
grunniens [30521]-40,588–20,241,016.fasta, protein entry ID: 40588). In DIA-NN, the allowance was one missed cleavage at most, with both precursor and fragment mass tolerances set to ±10 ppm. Cysteine residue carbamidomethylation was defined as a fixed modification, while methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation were considered variable, allowing up to one variable modification. The accepted peptide length was between 7 and 30 amino acids, with charge states ranging from 1 to 4, and the fragment ion
m
/
z
range was set from 150 to 2000. In the N-glycoproteomic workflow, Proteome Discoverer settings specified trypsin as the digestion enzyme, allowing a maximum of two missed cleavages, with a precursor mass tolerance of 4.5 ppm and fragment mass tolerance of 20 ppm. Fixed modifications included carbamidomethylation of cysteines, while variable modifications included N-terminal acetylation, methionine oxidation, and asparagine deamidation (
18
O labeling). False discovery rate (FDR) was controlled at <1 % for peptide and protein levels in DIA-NN, and at the site, peptide spectrum match, and protein levels in Proteome Discoverer, with a minimum score of 40 required for modified peptides.
2.8
Bioinformatics analysis
Perseus software v2.1.5 (
Tyanova et al., 2016
), Microsoft Excel 2016, and R statistical computing software (version 3.6.3) were employed for bioinformatics data analyses. To ensure comparability of protein intensities between the YC and YM groups, intensity values were normalized by median centering across samples, and missing values were imputed with a constant value corresponding to half of the minimum observed intensity. For quantitative comparison of MFGM proteins and N-glycosylation sites between YC and YM, two-tailed Student's
t
-tests were performed in Perseus. Differentially expressed MFGM proteins (DEPs) were defined as those with a fold change ≥2 and
P
< 0.05, and differential N-glycosylation sites were defined as those with fold change >1 and
P
< 0.05. Hierarchical clustering analysis was performed using the pheatmap package in R with Euclidean distance and complete-linkage clustering. Functional annotation of protein sequences was based on data retrieved from UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot (
Boutet et al., 2016
), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) (
Kanehisa et al., 2012
), and Gene Ontology (GO) (
Ashburner et al., 2000
). Fisher's exact test was utilized for GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses, and FDR correction was applied for multiple comparisons. GO terms were categorized into biological process (BP), molecular function (MF), and cellular component (CC) (
Ashburner et al., 2000
). Enriched GO terms and KEGG pathways were regarded as statistically significant with
P
< 0.05.

Introduction
The yak (
Bos grunniens
), a keystone species of the Tibetan Plateau, plays a central role in the subsistence of high-altitude communities by providing essential resources such as milk, meat, fiber, and fuel (
Li et al., 2023
). Yak milk is not only consumed directly but is also processed by local herders into various traditional products, including butter, cheese, yogurt, and Tibetan tea (
Zhang et al., 2024
). Compared to other types of milk, yak milk is recognized for its richer and more diverse nutritional profile (
Wang et al., 2023
). Colostrum is the first milk produced after parturition and is particularly rich in immune-related components, including immunoglobulins, cytokines, and growth factors (
Sangild et al., 2021
;
Zhang, J. et al., 2022
). While colostrum is critical for shielding newborns from infections during the early stages of life, mature milk is primarily responsible for meeting the energy and nutritional needs necessary for continued growth and development (
Duan et al., 2024
). Despite the well-established importance of both colostrum and mature milk, the molecular differences between these two types of milk remain poorly understood, especially in species such as the yak, which is adapted to extreme environmental conditions.
Milk proteins are generally divided into casein, whey, and milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) proteins based on their distribution and solubility (
Chen et al., 2023
). Among these, MFGM is a complex trilayer membrane structure originating from the endoplasmic reticulum and apical plasma membrane that consists of multiple components, mainly membrane-specific proteins, glycoproteins, enzymes, neutral lipids, and polar lipids (
Li et al., 2024
;
Wilmot et al., 2024
). MFGM proteins account for approximately 1 %–4 % of total milk proteins and play a crucial role in maintaining the physical stability of milk fat globules (
Lv et al., 2024
).
As a type of glycosylation in which carbohydrate chains are connected to the nitrogen atom of asparagine residues within the protein backbone, N-glycosylation is pivotal for regulating protein stability, folding, and biomolecular interactions (
Pasala et al., 2024
). The synthesis and secretion of milk proteins by mammary epithelial cells during lactation are accompanied by N-glycosylation modifications, a prominently prevalent and multifaceted post-translational modification in milk, which not only maintains the proper protein conformation but also contributes to physiological functions such as anti-pathogenicity, promotion of probiotic colonization, and immune regulation (
Guan et al., 2023a
).
Recently, site-specific glycoproteomic technology platforms have been extensively utilized to map the N-glycosylation landscape of milk proteins. Studies by
Cao et al. (2018)
, Guan et al. (2023a), and
Zhao et al. (2024)
have employed these techniques to identify N-glycosylation sites in the MFGM proteins of humans, donkeys, and pigs, respectively. However, such site-specific N-glycoproteomic studies have not yet been conducted in yaks, despite their unique adaptation to extreme high-altitude environments.
Yaks reside in extremely high-altitude regions characterized by low oxygen concentrations, low temperatures, and severe climatic conditions (
Li et al., 2023
), face unique physiological challenges, including those affecting lactation (
Kong et al., 2021
). Hypoxic conditions can alter metabolic pathways in the mammary gland (
Kong et al., 2021
), while limited nutritional availability places high demands on maternal energy and immune adaptation during milk production. These environmental pressures may drive the evolution of specialized proteins and distinct glycosylation patterns in yak milk, which are potentially adapted to these stressors. Consequently, yak milk represents a valuable model for investigating the functional and structural properties of milk proteins and their post-translational modifications.
In summary, this study provides a comprehensive characterization of the MFGM proteome and N-glycosylation differences between yak colostrum (YC) and mature milk (YM). By comparing these two physiologically distinct milk types, the study aimed to 1) identify variations in protein composition and glycosylation patterns; 2) advance our understanding of lactation biology and milk adaptation in yaks living under high-altitude conditions; and 3) offer insights that may support the development of functional dairy products and the identification of potential nutritional and immunological biomarkers.

). Fisher's exact test was utilized for GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses, and FDR correction was applied for multiple comparisons. GO terms were categorized into biological process (BP), molecular function (MF), and cellular component (CC) (
Ashburner et al., 2000
). Enriched GO terms and KEGG pathways were regarded as statistically significant with
P
< 0.05.
3
Results and discussion
Before proteomic analyses, the basic composition of the pooled YC and YM samples was determined (Table S1). YC contained markedly higher levels of protein (19.35 ± 0.55 % vs. 4.50 ± 0.04 %), milk fat (6.73 ± 0.18 % vs. 3.20 ± 0.12 %) and IgG (94.61 ± 0.68 vs. 1.03 ± 0.03 mg/mL) than YM, whereas YM showed a higher lactose content (5.62 ± 0.14 % vs. 3.30 ± 0.07 %). These differences are consistent with the typical transition from concentrated, immune-rich colostrum to mature milk that provides more carbohydrate for sustained energy supply.
3.1
Identification of MFGM proteins in YC and YM
The Astral-DIA proteomic approach was used to profile MFGM proteins in YC and YM. Proteins were considered reliably identified if they contained at least two unique peptides and were detected in at least two out of three biological replicates in each group. A total of 4278 proteins were identified (Table S2). Of these, 3908 MFGM proteins were found in both groups, while 246 and 124 were uniquely expressed in YC and YM milk, respectively. Compared with previous studies,
Zhang, L. et al. (2022)
identified 1639 MFGM proteins in goat colostrum and mature milk using a shotgun proteomic approach.
Li et al. (2019)
reported 2762 MFGM proteins in donkey milk based on a label-free quantification strategy.
Zhao et al. (2023)
employed label-free proteomics to identify 3807 MFGM proteins in porcine colostrum and mature milk, with 110 and 159 proteins uniquely expressed in colostrum and mature milk, respectively. These studies revealed that MFGM proteins across species are dynamically regulated during lactation and play vital roles in immune protection, lipid metabolism, and structural maintenance of milk fat globules, reflecting species-specific physiological adaptations and nutritional characteristics of milk. Compared with these studies, our analysis identified a larger number of MFGM proteins. This higher coverage is likely related to the increased analytical depth and sensitivity of the workflow, as well as potential species-specific differences in MFGM composition between yaks and other dairy animals. The results of hierarchical clustering analysis demonstrated high consistency among biological replicates (Fig. S1). Consistently, the principal component analysis (PCA) score plot (
Fig. 1
A) indicated that the three replicates within each group clustered closely together, while YC and YM were clearly separated, confirming good reproducibility and distinct proteomic profiles between the two lactation stages.

3.2
Differentially expressed MFGM proteins in YC and YM
Based on the criteria of
P
< 0.05 and fold change ≥2, a total of 1271 DEPs were identified between YC and YM (Table S3). Among these, 1091 were commonly expressed in both groups, while 112 and 68 proteins were uniquely detected in YC and YM, respectively. These group-specific proteins may serve as potential biomarkers for further investigation. Compared with YC, 590 MFGM proteins were upregulated and 681 MFGM proteins were downregulated in YM (
Fig. 1
B). In comparison, Zhang, L. et al. (2022),
Li et al. (2019)
, and
Zhao et al. (2023)
identified 232, 61, and 303 DEPs in goat, donkey, and porcine MFGM proteomes under the same criteria, respectively. Among them, 131, 47, and 129 proteins were upregulated, while 101, 14, and 174 were downregulated in mature milk compared with colostrum. Consistent with the higher overall protein coverage described above, a larger number of DEPs was also detected in this study. This may be partly related to the earlier colostrum sampling time. While previous studies collected colostrum samples over several days postpartum, the present study employed samples obtained within 2 h after parturition, which likely ensured a more accurate representation of true colostrum composition and contributed to the increased number of DEPs.
The volcano plot displays the top 10 DEPs ranked by
P
-value (
Fig. 1
C), and the complex heatmap of the top 50 DEPs with total expression intensity is shown in
Fig. 1
D. Several major MFGM proteins showed significant differential expression between YC and YM, including those involved in lipid and energy metabolism, structural integrity, and immune function. Fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs), such as FABP3 (
Q4TZH2
) and FABP7 (A0A8B9X2U5), were significantly upregulated in YM. FABPs are a family of highly conserved proteins that play crucial roles in lipid-mediated processes and metabolic pathways (
Furuhashi et al., 2008
), among which FABP3 is essential for transporting fatty acids, a process critical for mammary lipid synthesis during lactation (
Bionaz et al., 2008
). Similarly, mucins MUC1 (A0A8C0AFE0) and MUC15 (A0A8B9Y2Y3), key glycoproteins of the MFGM, also exhibited elevated expression in YM, contributing to membrane protection (
Lane et al., 2012
;
Ortega-Anaya et al., 2022
). These findings are consistent with the results of
Reinhardt et al. (2008)
, who reported higher expression of FABP and MUC1 in day 7 milk than in colostrum in Holsteins. Colostrum generally has a higher fat content, yet FABP expression is lower in early lactation (
Manoni et al., 2020
;
Reinhardt et al., 2008
). This pattern may reflect a metabolic transition in lipid handling as lactation is initiated.
L-lactate dehydrogenase (LDH, A0A8B9W9Z6), a key enzyme catalyzing the conversion of lactate to pyruvate (
Adeva et al., 2013
), was significantly downregulated in YM, possibly suggesting a decreased reliance on glycolysis in the mammary gland as lactation progresses. In contrast, galactokinase 2 (GALK2, A0A8B9XII2), which plays a central role in lactose biosynthesis (
Mohammad et al., 2012
), was upregulated in YM, consistent with the higher lactose content observed in YM compared to YC (5.62 ± 0.14 % vs. 3.30 ± 0.07 %, respectively). These opposing expression trends may indicate a metabolic shift from high-energy colostrum to sustained milk synthesis with enhanced lactose output. Additionally, Ig-like domain-containing protein (A0A8B9YLQ7), a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily involved in immune recognition and signaling (
Chagas et al., 2024
), was significantly downregulated in YM, consistent with prior findings in cows (
Feng et al., 2023
). This decline may reflect the prioritization of immune defense in colostrum to support adaptation of neonatal calves immediately after birth.
3.3
Functional annotation and enrichment analyses of differentially expressed MFGM proteins
To further analyze the functions of the DEPs between the YC and YM groups, GO annotations were conducted. The identified DEPs were associated with BP including negative regulation of peptidase activity, cell adhesion, and negative regulation of endopeptidase activity. In terms of CC enrichment, MFGM proteins were primarily localized to the extracellular region, extracellular space, and cell periphery. Regarding MF, these proteins were mainly involved in molecular transducer activity, signaling receptor activity, and transmembrane signaling receptor activity (
Fig. 2
). These annotations highlight functional shifts in MFGM proteins across lactation stages and provide a reference for further investigation into yak milk bioactivity.

KEGG pathway analysis revealed 81 significantly enriched pathways (
q
-value <0.05), with the top 10 shown in
Fig. 3
A. Among these, complement and coagulation cascades (map04610), focal adhesion (map04510), and lysosome (map04142) were the most significantly enriched. Notably, the complement and coagulation cascades was also reported to be enriched in goat milk MFGM proteins by
Liang et al. (2024)
. This pathway is crucial for linking innate immunity with hemostasis (
Keragala et al., 2018
). As a central component of innate immunity, the complement system can be activated via classical, lectin, and alternative pathways (
Ning et al., 2023
), among which the classical pathway relies on antigen-antibody complexes (e.g., IgG or IgM bound to pathogens) for its activation (
Daha et al., 2011
). In the present study, colostrum exhibited elevated IgG levels (94.61 ± 0.68 mg/mL) compared to mature milk (1.03 ± 0.03 mg/mL), along with increased abundance of classical complement pathway components, including C1s (A0A8B9Y721), C2 (A0A8C0AGK7), C5 (A0A8B9XH04), and C8 subunits (A0A8C0A2C5 and A0A8B9W1X7). These findings indicated that IgG-mediated classical complement activation might play an important role in the passive immune defense of neonatal calves through colostrum.

Of the 35 DEPs involved in the complement and coagulation cascades, most were downregulated in YM. However, fibrinogen beta chain (FGB, A0A8B9Y5E0), fibrinogen gamma chain (FGG, A0A8B9Y007), protein C receptor (PROCR, A0A8B9X2K4), and membrane cofactor protein (MCP, A0A8B9X4T2) were upregulated. These proteins are involved in the regulation of coagulation and inflammatory processes (
Kim et al., 2006
;
Kishi et al., 2016
;
Simurda et al., 2020
). The upregulation of these proteins may support the transition from immune defense in colostrum to tissue repair during lactation, reflecting a potential adaptive strategy of yaks in high-altitude environments.
According to KEGG level 2 classification, the majority of these significantly enriched pathways were related to the immune system (
Fig. 3
B). In addition to complement and coagulation cascades, other immune-related pathways include phagosome, Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis (map04666), and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation (map04613) were significantly enriched. Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis links IgG-bound pathogens to phagocytes (
Junker et al., 2020
), and may reinforce passive immunity in calves. Although NET formation is less well-characterized in milk, it may act as a secondary barrier against microbial dissemination by entrapping pathogens through DNA-based scaffolds and releasing antimicrobial peptides (
Zawrotniak et al., 2013
). The combined effect of these pathways might enhance the protective ability of colostrum.
3.4
Identification of N-Glycoproteome in YC and YM
A 4D label-free glycoproteomic approach was employed to characterize N-glycosylation modifications of MFGM proteins in YC and YM. The PCA showed no clear separation between the two groups (Fig. S2), indicating limited overall differences in their N-glycoproteome profiles. A total of 89 N-glycoproteins, 120 N-glycopeptides, and 128 N-glycosylation sites were identified (Table S4). Compared with other species, the number of glycosylated components identified in this study was relatively lower. Guan et al. (2023b) reported 1677 N-glycopeptides corresponding to 506 glycosylation sites on 326 glycoproteins in donkey MFGM, and 3153 N-glycopeptides mapped to 550 sites on 328 glycoproteins in human MFGM. These studies have demonstrated that N-glycoproteins are involved in critical biological functions such as immune response modulation, cell signaling, and metabolic regulation during lactation, highlighting their potential roles in shaping species-specific milk functionality and supporting neonatal adaptation. The relatively lower number of N-glycoproteins identified in yak milk likely reflects species-specific variation in milk glycosylation complexity. In addition, the lectin mixture (ConA, WGA, RCA120) used for N-glycopeptide enrichment exhibits specificity for high-mannose, hybrid, and certain complex glycans (
Riley et al., 2021
), which may have contributed to the lower number of identified glycopeptides. Although N-glycosylation in yak whey proteins has been previously investigated (
Zhong et al., 2024
), little information is available regarding glycosylation in yak MFGM proteins. Therefore,the present study provides the N-glycoproteomic dataset of yak MFGM, thus filling a knowledge gap and offering a foundation for further investigation in high-altitude adapted species.
Among the identified N-glycoproteins in this study, 69 (77.5 %) were single N-glycosylated, 12 (13.5 %) were double N-glycosylated, and 8 (9 %) were multiple N-glycosylated. Highly N-glycosylated proteins include Xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase (XDH/XO, A0A8C0A6L7, N351, N261, N556, N768, N956, N11), Alpha-S2-casein (A0A8B9Z540, N156, N80, N43, N139, N118, N115), Fatty acid synthase (A0A8C0A6C4, N2238, N1265, N1985, N906, N2221), and Alpha-S1-casein (A0A344X7B7, N199, N129, N34, N32, N154). XDH/XO is primarily found in MFGM and extracellular vesicles, where it predominantly exists in the oxidase form and catalyzes the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and uric acid, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and hydrogen peroxide in the process (
Gadegaard et al., 2025
). Its multiple glycosylation sites may enhance protein stability and protect catalytic sites from oxidative damage, thereby contributing to redox homeostasis under hypoxic conditions typical of high-altitude environments. Milk caseins serve diverse functions, such as supplying amino acids and calcium, and contributing to immune regulation (
Vordenbäumen et al., 2016
; Yang et al., 2016a). Human α-S1-casein has been shown to support immune system maturation and promote sustained IgG production in nursing infants (
Vordenbäumen et al., 2016
;
Zhang et al., 2021
), while glycosylated and phosphorylated forms of α-S1-casein have been observed in donkey milk (
Bertino et al., 2010
). The high level of glycosylation observed in yak caseins in this study may enhance micelle stability and support protein functionality during lactation. Such extensively glycosylated MFGM components may be particularly advantageous under chronic hypoxia and oxidative stress at high altitude, by helping to stabilize milk structures and support neonatal adaptation, although this possibility remains to be tested in comparative studies.
Based on the signal intensities of the identified N-glycopeptides, the abundances of glycosylated sites and N-glycoproteins were quantified. For reliable quantification, only glycopeptides detected in at least two of three replicates were included in the final analysis. Under this filtering criterion, a total of 18 N-glycosylation sites, 15 N-glycopeptides, and 13 N-glycoproteins were collectively quantified in YC and YM groups. 10 N-glycosylation sites, 9 N-glycopeptides, and 7 N-glycoproteins were individually identified in YC MFGM proteins, and 8 N-glycosylation sites, 7 N-glycopeptides, and 4 N-glycoproteins were individually identified in YM MFGM proteins (
Fig. 4
).

3.5
Differential N-glycosylation sites in YC and YM
Among all identified N-glycosylation sites, only the N50 glycosylation site on UBX domain protein 6 (UBXN6, A0A8B9XPC1) was significantly downregulated in YM compared to YC (
P
< 0.05, fold change >1) (Table S5) This finding indicates that N-glycosylation differences between lactation stages may be limited at the site-specific level, suggesting a relatively stable N-glycoproteome during the transition from colostrum to mature milk.
Notably, the total protein abundance of UBXN6 remained unchanged, implying that the N50 site may function as an independent regulatory element. UBXN6 functions as an adaptor protein in the endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway, which maintains proteostasis by targeting misfolded proteins for degradation (
Kim et al., 2024
). The decreased glycosylation at N50 in YM may reflect stage-specific modulation of ER quality control activity in the mammary gland. During early lactation, mammary epithelial cells exhibit elevated secretory activity and ER stress (
Davis et al., 2016
;
Sangild et al., 2021
;
Yonekura et al., 2018
), which may increase the demand for glycosylation to support protein folding. As lactation progresses, a shift toward casein and lipid synthesis likely reduces this burden (
Chen et al., 2024
;
Rudolph et al., 2007
), potentially explaining the observed decrease in glycosylation at N50. In addition to its role in proteostasis, UBXN6 has been implicated in immune regulation.
Kim et al. (2024)
demonstrated that UBXN6 modulates inflammatory responses by promoting autophagy and maintaining immune homeostasis, particularly in macrophages. The altered glycosylation at N50 may influence UBXN6 interactions with immune-related pathways, such as p97-mediated autophagy or ERAD, potentially contributing to the adaptation of immune function in early lactation. This site-specific glycosylation change could play a role in modulating the immune functions of MFGM proteins, potentially contributing to immune adaptation under high-altitude conditions. But this interpretation requires further investigation.
Interestingly, several enzymes involved in N-glycosylation such as Dol-P-Man:Man(5)GlcNAc(2)-PP-Dol alpha-1,3-mannosyltransferase (ALG3, A0A8B9W6B9), mannosyltransferase (ALG9, A0A8B9X7V1), UDP-
N
-acetylglucosamine–dolichyl-phosphate
N
-acetylglucosaminephosphotransferase (DPAGT1, A0A8B9XV14), and dolichyl-diphosphooligosaccharide–protein glycotransferase (STT3B, A0A8B9YUV7) were found to be upregulated in YM. ALG3 and ALG9 are mannosyltransferases involved in the early steps of dolichol-linked oligosaccharide synthesis (
Tham et al., 2016
), while DPAGT1 and STT3B are essential for glycan transfer to nascent polypeptides (
Harada et al., 2022
;
Kanaki et al., 2018
). However, the reduced glycosylation observed at UBXN6-N50 suggests that local glycan processing, rather than core glycan assembly, may be the limiting factor for site-specific glycosylation at this stage.
In contrast, beta-galactoside alpha-(2,6)-sialyltransferase (ST6GAL1, A0A8B9W9H5) and N-acylneuraminate cytidylyltransferase (CMAS, A0A8B9WH02) as key enzymes involved in sialic acid biosynthesis and transfer, were downregulated in YM (
Ma et al., 2024
). ST6GAL1 catalyzes α2,6-linked sialylation (
Gc et al., 2022
), and CMAS is required for the activation of sialic acid to CMP-sialic acid (
Jame-Chenarboo et al., 2025
). Lower expression of these enzymes may reduce the extent of terminal sialylation on glycoproteins such as UBXN6, possibly contributing to the decreased occupancy at the N50 site. However, this interpretation should be considered a hypothesis generated from the current data, and further experimental validation is needed to confirm the proposed mechanism.
In the MFGM proteome, UBX domain-containing protein 4 (UBXN4, A0A8B9W9G8) and vesicle-fusing ATPase (NSF, A0A8B9YAX5), both of which interact with UBXN6, are also differentially regulated. UBXN4 is a member of the UBX domain protein family, but it may tend to regulate mitophagy (
Spena et al., 2022
;
Sulkshane et al., 2021
), while NSF is a SNARE complex dissociating enzyme that regulates membrane fusion events (
Ryu et al., 2015
). Upregulation of UBXN4 and NSF in YM enhances mitophagy and membrane fusion, respectively. The upregulation of these proteins in YM may suggest that UBXN6 and its associated proteins perform distinct functions at different lactation stages, which may be influenced by post-translational modifications including glycosylation.
Overall, although UBXN6-N50 was the only significantly altered N-glycosylation site, the N-glycoproteome remained relatively stable between YC and YM. This contrasts with the dynamic changes observed in the proteome, suggesting that different layers of regulation operate at the expression and modification levels. While protein abundance may adapt to changing metabolic and immune demands during lactation, N-glycosylation may serve as a more conserved mechanism to maintain MFGM structure and function across stages.
3.6
Functional annotation and enrichment analyses of MFGM N-glycoproteins
To investigate the biological roles of MFGM N-glycoproteins, proteins with>50 % missing values in the same group were excluded, resulting in 25 proteins undergoing GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis (Table S6). Functional enrichment revealed that these proteins were mainly involved in biological regulation, response to external stimulus, and regulation of immune response. Under the CC category, extracellular space, extracellular region, and membrane raft were the top three terms according to the
P
-value. Further, the majority of identified N-glycoproteins were annotated with MF of immunoglobulin receptor binding, guanyl-nucleotide exchange factor activity, and enzyme regulator activity (
Fig. 5
). Subcellular localization annotations showed that 46.15 % of the glycoproteins were located in the extracellular region, 30.77 % on the membrane, and 23.08 % in the cytoplasm (Fig. S3). These results indicate that MFGM glycoproteins are mainly involved in immune defense and cell communication, which are essential for neonatal calf development.

Among the 20 pathways significantly enriched by N-glycoproteins, the majority were associated with three key proteins: immunoglobulin heavy constant mu (IGHM, A0A8B9WYU5), monocyte differentiation antigen CD14 (CD14, A0A8B9XYM9), and platelet glycoprotein 4 (CD36, A0A8B9Y3N1), with IGHM contributing most prominently. CD14 and CD36 are members of the class B receptor family, involved in immune responses by regulating antigen recognition and phagocytosis by immune cells (
Xiao et al., 2022
). Notably, CD36 has been identified as a conserved MFGM N-glycoprotein in the colostrum and mature milk of both donkeys and humans (Guan et al., 2023b). Collectively, these N-glycoproteins are likely to contribute to the innate immune defense mechanisms of YC, supporting immune development in neonatal calves.
In addition, 12 of these 20 pathways overlap with those enriched in the MFGM proteome, including the phagosome, mineral absorption, and Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis pathways, suggesting that N-glycosylation may act synergistically with protein abundance to regulate key biological processes during the transition from YC to YM. As reported by Guan et al. (2023b), the phagosome pathway ranked among the top three significantly enriched KEGG pathways associated with MFGM glycoproteins in both colostrum and mature milk from donkeys and humans. Phagocytosis plays an essential role in tissue homeostasis and host defense by mediating the clearance of apoptotic vesicles, senescent cells, and pathogens (
Shrivastava et al., 2022
). The significant enrichment of MFGM glycoproteins in the phagosome pathway underscores their importance in neonatal mammalian physiology. In our dataset, N-glycoproteins such as IGHM, CD14, and CD36, as well as other MFGM proteins including V-type proton ATPase subunits (A0A8B9Z4K0, A0A8B9X200, A0A8B9X8U1) and RAC1(A0A8B9YQE2), were also enriched in this pathway. These proteins play essential roles in phagosomal acidification and membrane remodeling during particle internalization (
Castellano et al., 2000
;
Kissing et al., 2018
). These findings highlight a potential interplay between N-glycosylation and protein expression that may enhance the immunological competency of yak milk during early lactation.
Overall, the enrichment of immune-related pathways and N-glycoproteins in yak colostrum suggests a strong protective function for neonatal calves. While such immune features may enhance pathogen resistance, especially under high-altitude conditions, it remains unclear whether these proteomic patterns are yak-specific or reflect general bovine lactation responses. Therefore, the present findings should be interpreted within the context of this particular yak population and management system, and comparative studies involving different breeds and production environments are needed to further validate these observations.
4
Conclusion
In conclusion, this study comprehensively profiled MFGM proteins and their associated N-glycoproteins in YC and YM. In total, 1271 different expressed MFGM proteins and 128 N-glycosylation sites on 89 glycoproteins were identified. While the proteome exhibited substantial changes between YC and YM, the N-glycoproteome remained relatively stable at the site-specific level, suggesting different modes of regulation between protein abundance and glycosylation during lactation. GO functional annotations and KEGG pathway analysis revealed the commonalities and distinctions in biological functions of MFGM proteins and N-glycoproteins between YC and YM, revealed the potential relationship between the N-glycosylation pattern and biological functions of yak MFGM glycoproteins. This study expanded our understanding of the yak MFGM proteome and N-glycoproteome and provided a reference for the development of functional products from yak milk resources, within the context of the specific yak population and production conditions examined. However, this study focused primarily on the differences between YC and YM in terms of MFGM N-glycosylation. To expand the dataset and gain a deeper understanding of the chemical modifications of yak MFGM proteins, future research should explore site-specific N-glycosylation and other post-translational modifications. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the role of MFGM glycosylation in immune function and other physiological processes.
